title: Define mastery with worked answers and a rubric
statement: Define a mastery task by worked answers and a rubric that scores the whole performance, rather than by a list of sub-skills.
example: On one draft rubric each of four rows is scored 1 to 4, and an answer meets the bar only with every row at 3 or higher.
detail: A Grade 3 demonstration unit defines its capstone, understanding an unseen passage on the unit's topic, by exemplars and a rubric rather than by decomposing it further. The draft shows an answer that meets the bar and one that exceeds it, each annotated row by row, and a below-the-bar answer that recites topic knowledge a student could write without reading the passage. Its four-row rubric is met only when every row scores 3 or higher, so an answer cannot pass by excelling on one row and failing another.
against: The rubric is a draft, not an approved scoring key, and no capstone was published (`grade3-reading/artifacts/demo-unit-2026-07-10/phase-e/capstone/exemplars-rubric.md`, lines 14-16); the 10 selected-response capstone items all failed the anti-leak gate ("certified": 0, `grade3-reading/artifacts/demo-unit-2026-07-10/phase-e/capstone/gate-capstone-summary.json`, line 13), a verdict the draft says neither approves nor rejects the rubric.

evidence.quote: the mastery performance; defined by exemplars + rubric, NOT decomposed further
SHOWING two worked responses and a rubric that scores the whole performance, instead of splitting mastery into atomised sub-skills.
Why this is NOT YET: recites world/topic knowledge
Score each row 1-4. "Meets the capstone" = every row at 3 or higher
each SCR declares the cut *and* carries a **borderline** exemplar at that cut — not only a top-score model — so "meets" is anchored where the decision is actually hard.
